opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. In my own experience, there's often a real tension between the two.

On one side, machine learning has become extraordinarily good at simply *getting things done*. You have a task, you collect enough data, you train a large enough model, and it works, often better than anything we could have engineered by hand. From a practical standpoint that's very powerful. If your goal is a product or solving a concrete problem, you may not need to know why it works, as long as it works reliably.

But I've always felt that something is lost if we stop there. When you understand the underlying principles, why a phenomenon happens, what structure in the data the model is exploiting, you gain things a black-box solution doesn't give you. You can predict when it will fail. You can transfer the insight to a new problem. And sometimes the understanding is more valuable than the task itself, because it changes how you see a whole class of problems.

So I don't see them as opposites. I'd say they're complementary, and the most interesting work happens in the back-and-forth. Often you build something that works first, and that success becomes the object of study. Why did it work? What did the model learn? In some sense the trained model becomes a new kind of experimental system, almost like a natural phenomenon we can probe. Conversely, when you understand the principles, you can design better models, choose better inductive biases, and use data more efficiently.

The danger is going too far in either direction. If you only chase performance, you can end up with systems that are brittle in ways you don't anticipate, and the field can drift into incremental benchmark-climbing. If you only insist on first-principles understanding, you might miss what's empirically possible, because a lot of what deep learning has shown us came from trying things that theory wouldn't have predicted.

Personally, I lean toward wanting to understand. Getting a result is satisfying, but the moment I find most rewarding is when something clicks and I can say, "Ah, that's *why*." But I've learned to respect the empirical side. Sometimes you have to let the system show you what's possible before you know what questions to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says machine learning can get a task done powerfully without knowing why it works, and treats that practical success as valuable.

r002.rationale: It discusses predicting failures and the value of understanding, but does not propose research to establish guarantees for solutions developed without that understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually one of the most interesting tensions in the field right now, and I don't think it's a tradeoff in the way people usually frame it.

The common framing is: you can either throw a huge model at a problem and get the answer without understanding why, or you can do the slow, careful work of understanding the mechanism and get something interpretable but maybe less capable. And then people line up on one side or the other. The engineers say, who cares about understanding, it works. The scientists say, if you don't understand it, you haven't really solved anything.

My own view is that these two things feed each other, and the interesting work happens at the boundary. When I started working on language models, a lot of what we did was essentially empirical. You train the thing, you look at the loss curve, you try to make the number go down. And honestly, that got us very far. Scaling laws came out of that kind of empiricism. Nobody derived them from first principles. They were observed.

But what I noticed is that every time we hit a wall, the thing that got us through was some piece of understanding. Not necessarily deep theory, but a mechanistic intuition about what the model was actually doing. Why does attention help with long-range dependencies? Why do certain training instabilities show up at certain scales? If you have even a rough model of that, you can make the next empirical step much more efficiently. Without it, you're doing random search in a very expensive space.

So I'd put it this way. Accomplishing the task gives you evidence. Understanding gives you leverage on that evidence. If you only have the first, you're stuck repeating whatever worked last time and hoping it generalizes. If you only have the second, you often find your beautiful theory doesn't survive contact with real data.

There's also a practical point about who you're working with. When I'm talking to people on the product side, they genuinely don't need the mechanism. They need to know whether it works, how reliably, and what it costs. That's a legitimate way to use machine learning and I don't think it's lesser. But when something goes wrong, and something always goes wrong, the people who understood the system are the ones who can fix it rather than just retrain and pray.

The thing I worry about a little bit is that the field is getting so good at the first mode, accomplishing the task, that the second mode starts to look like a luxury. Interpretability research is still a small fraction of what gets done. And the models are getting harder to understand faster than our tools for understanding them are improving. That gap concerns me more than any single capability question.

So if I had to give a short answer: I don't optimize for one or the other. I try to keep both running in parallel, and I treat the moments where the empirical result surprises me as the most valuable signal, because that's exactly where my understanding was wrong and where there's something new to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says product users may only need to know whether a machine-learning system works, and calls that a legitimate use that is not lesser—even when they do not need to understand its mechanism.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the value of understanding and interpretability, but does not propose research to establish guarantees for solutions developed without understanding underlying principles.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two related but different goals. If your goal is to accomplish a task, then a machine-learning system that works reliably can be valuable even if you don’t fully understand why it works. You shouldn’t dismiss that practical achievement.

But successfully performing a task doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve understood the underlying principles. A model might predict a physical phenomenon very accurately without giving us an explanation of what causes it. And that distinction becomes important when we move beyond the conditions represented in the training data.

So I wouldn’t make it an either-or choice. We can use machine learning to discover patterns and generate hypotheses, then test those hypotheses to develop a deeper understanding. The question is what we want from the result: a useful prediction, an explanation, or both.

r001.rationale: It says a reliable machine-learning system can be valuable even when we do not fully understand why it works, and calls that a practical achievement.

r002.rationale: It suggests testing hypotheses to gain deeper understanding, but does not propose research into whether guarantees can be established for solutions whose principles are not understood.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are two related but distinct goals. You can build a machine learning system that performs a task very well without fully understanding why it works. That’s valuable in itself, but success on a task doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve understood the underlying phenomenon.

Understanding becomes especially important when we want to predict where the system will fail, or whether it will work under different conditions. So I wouldn’t insist that we understand everything before building something useful. I’d let the two approaches inform each other: build systems, study their successes and failures, and use what we learn to develop better explanations. The key is to be clear about which kind of progress we’ve actually made.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a system can perform a task very well without full understanding, and that achievement is valuable in itself.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses understanding failures and behavior under different conditions, but does not propose research to establish guarantees for solutions built without understanding.
